prompt.context: Our client, Bun on the Run, operates a fast food restaurant chain. The industry's average profit margin is 3 to 5%. However, our client currently is making only 1.5%.
prompt.question: How can you help them increase their margins to 3%?

clarifying_info.a: The fast food outlets are on toll roads and in airports.

clarifying_info.q: Are the outlets company-owned or franchised?
Which part of the business is underperforming?
clarifying_info.a: Airports constitute most of their business, and the low profit margins are due to the airport business.

clarifying_info.q: What is the state of the industry?
clarifying_info.a: The industry is fairly mature and stagnant.

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's market share?
clarifying_info.a: The client operates in 80% of airports and is present in all large airports, servicing 90% of all airport passengers.
There is only one other competitor with the remaining 10% market share; their margins are on par with the industry average.

clarifying_info.q: What does the menu look like?
clarifying_info.a: Standard fast food menu; competitor is no different.

clarifying_info.q: What does the cost structure look like?
clarifying_info.a: Variable costs are 70% (COGS 35%, Labor 35%). Fixed costs are 30% (Airport fee 10%, Infrastructure 5%, Rent 15%).

Core ingredients (bread, meat, etc.) are 70% of COGS and are already optimized — costs cannot be cut further. Non-core ingredients (paper towels, ketchup, etc.) are 30% of COGS and are contracted through SYSCO at competitive rates.

clarifying_info.q: Tell me more about labor costs.
clarifying_info.a: Most employees are salaried and full time, earning minimum wage of $6/hour. Benefits start after 6 months. Turnover is 200%. A new employee costs an additional $18/hour, which includes training (4 weeks) and a background check.

framework: Revenue: assess whether pricing, volume, or mix can be improved given mature/stagnant market and near-monopoly position
Cost — Variable (70%): break down COGS (35%) and Labor (35%) for reduction opportunities
Cost — Fixed (30%): review airport fees (10%), infrastructure (5%), and rent (15%) for renegotiation or optimization
Identify the primary cost driver: zero in on labor given the 200% turnover rate and high onboarding cost
Root cause: employees trained at client's expense then leave for higher-wage competitors (e.g., nearby McDonald's)
Solution: reduce turnover / increase retention to lower effective labor cost and restore margin

questions.prompt: Walk through the cost structure and identify which line item is the primary drag on margins.
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure costs into variable (70%) and fixed (30%). Within variable, Labor at 35% is equal to COGS at 35%). COGS is already optimized (core ingredients cannot be cut; non-core contracted at competitive rates). Labor is therefore the lever. Candidate should ask about labor specifics and surface the 200% turnover as the key issue.

math.setup: Understand the incremental cost per new hire: base wage $6/hr + training/hiring cost $18/hr = $24/hr effective cost during training. With 200% annual turnover, the workforce is replaced twice per year, multiplying the $18/hr premium across the entire headcount twice annually.
steps: Effective cost during training period = $6 (wage) + $18 (training & background check) = $24/hr
Excess cost per new hire per training hour = $18/hr
At 200% turnover the entire workforce is replaced 2x per year, so training cost is incurred continuously and depresses margins materially
math.answer: The $18/hr training premium applied to a workforce turning over 200% annually is the primary driver of the labor cost problem.

questions.prompt: What recommendations would you make to reduce turnover and restore margins?
questions.guidance: Good: identify the turnover problem and propose reducing it (e.g., pay above minimum wage, accelerate benefits eligibility). Better: suggest making benefits available earlier (before 6 months) and paying slightly above minimum wage to compete with nearby higher-wage employers. Superior: propose low-cost retention mechanisms such as cross-training employees across stations to increase job satisfaction and engagement, while noting the trade-off that cross-training may temporarily reduce utilization.

brainstorming.prompt: What strategies could Bun on the Run use to increase employee retention with minimal additional cost?

categories.name: Compensation & Benefits
ideas: Pay marginally above minimum wage to differentiate from competing employers
Make benefits (health, etc.) available earlier than the current 6-month threshold
Introduce performance-based bonuses tied to tenure milestones

categories.name: Job Satisfaction & Career Development
ideas: Cross-train employees across multiple stations to reduce monotony and increase engagement
Create clear promotion pathways from crew to shift supervisor
Recognize top performers publicly (employee of the month, etc.)

categories.name: Hiring & Onboarding
ideas: Improve candidate screening to hire people more likely to stay
Reduce the 4-week training period where possible to lower cost per hire
Use referral bonuses to attract candidates through existing employees

categories.name: Work Environment
ideas: Improve scheduling flexibility to attract and retain workers with outside commitments
Foster a team culture that makes employees feel valued

categories.name: Structural / Operational
ideas: Explore automation of repetitive tasks to reduce headcount dependency
Negotiate with airport authorities for partial fee relief in exchange for service commitments
Benchmark non-core COGS contracts periodically despite current SYSCO arrangement

recommendation: The primary driver of Bun on the Run's below-industry margins (1.5% vs. 3-5% industry) is excessive labor cost caused by a 200% annual employee turnover rate; the $18/hr training-and-hiring premium applied to a constantly churning workforce is bleeding the margin

Immediate priority: reduce turnover by (1) making benefits available before the 6-month mark, (2) paying a modest premium above minimum wage to compete with nearby employers, and (3) implementing cross-training to raise job satisfaction at low incremental cost
risks: Paying above minimum wage raises the steady-state labor cost baseline — the margin benefit only materializes if the reduction in training costs outweighs the wage increase
Cross-training increases flexibility but may temporarily lower individual station utilization during the transition
Structural fixes (renegotiating airport fees or rent) may face long-term contractual constraints
next_steps: Quantify the break-even wage premium: calculate how much extra per hour in wages is justified by the savings from lower turnover and training costs
Pilot an early-benefits and cross-training program at a subset of airport locations and measure 90-day retention vs. control group
Conduct a lease/fee review across airport locations to identify any near-term renegotiation windows
